recall_prompt: Say how you would prove 9t = 16 — what you add to both sides, what you compare with, how you find p, q and x, and why the power comes out as a plain fraction 25/9.
insider_note: No leading 1 is printed, so add 1 on both sides first. The power is (3/5)⁻² = 25/9 — the negative index inverts the fraction, and writing 9/25 is the one slip that stops 9t = 16.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/5)ᵏ. No leading 1, so add 1 on both sides. The numerators 4, 4·6, 4·6·8 step by 2, so q = 2 and p/q = 2 is a whole number — the power is an ordinary square.

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/5) to the power k, after adding 1 on both sides so the missing early terms are present.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by five to the power k and add 1 on both sides
split each denominator into five to the power k times k factorial
add 1 to both sides and bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by five power k tho rayali, rendu sides ki 1 add cheyali
rewrite the denominators as powers of five times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − x)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio x/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and x cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1 on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 5.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − x) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into x by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into x by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
(1 − x)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and x
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (4), p + q is the second (6) so q = 2, and x/q equals the common ratio 1/5 so x = q/5 = 2/5.

recall.must_convey: That p = 4 and p + q = 6 give q = 2, and x/q = 1/5 gives x = two by five.
accept: p is four, p plus q is six so q is two, and x by q is one by five so x is two by five
the first factor gives p equal to four and the second gives q equal to two
x by q equals one by five so x equals two by five
p four, q two vasthai, x by q one by five kabatti x two by five
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes x/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking x = 1/5 directly — the bracket holds x/q, so x = q × 1/5.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, x into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives one plus t equals five by three squared, which is twenty five by nine.
accept: substituting gives one plus t equals five by three squared, which is twenty five by nine
put the values into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify to get one plus t equals five by three squared, which is twenty five by nine
the bracket becomes three by five and the power gives one plus t equals five by three squared, which is twenty five by nine

simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: one plus t equals five by three squared, which is twenty five by nine

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: Clear the fraction
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. Multiply by 9 and the 16 appears: 9 + 9t = 25.

accept: one plus t is twenty five by nine so nine plus nine t is twenty five and nine t is sixteen
multiply by nine and subtract nine to get sixteen
nine t equals sixteen

twenty five minus nine is sixteen

steps.why: Because p/q = 2 is a whole number, the power is a plain square and the result is a rational number — no roots at all in this one.
common_mistakes: Writing (3/5) to the power −2 as 9/25 instead of 25/9.
Reading q as 6 instead of p + q = 6.
